title.en: The Front Half of RAG: all-MiniLM-L6-v2 as Your Retriever

description.en: Build the retrieval half of a RAG pipeline with the world's most-downloaded embedding model: split documents into overlapping chunks, embed them with all-MiniLM-L6-v2, and pull the top-k most relevant chunks for any question â€” before an LLM ever sees a token.

story_variants.en:
## The LLM Never Reads Your Documents

"Here's the RAG secret nobody puts in the acronym," Vaathiyaar begins. "The language model never searches anything. A tiny 22-million-parameter embedding model â€” **all-MiniLM-L6-v2** â€” reads your documents first, decides which handful of passages matter, and the LLM only ever sees those. Get retrieval wrong and the smartest LLM on earth confidently answers from the wrong page. Today you build that front half yourself."

### Step 1: Chunk Before You Embed

MiniLM truncates input at 256 word pieces, and one vector per *whole document* blurs every topic inside it together. So RAG pipelines split documents into **chunks** â€” and they overlap the chunks so a sentence sitting on a boundary isn't torn in half:

| Chunking choice | What happens |
|---|---|
| Whole document, one vector | Truncated at 256 tokens; one blurry topic-average |
| Small chunks, no overlap | Boundary sentences split mid-thought; answers fall in the gap |
| Small chunks + overlap | Boundary content appears in two chunks â€” one of them keeps it intact |

A sliding window does it: take `size` words, step forward by `size - overlap`, repeat until you reach the end.

### Step 2: Embed and Retrieve

```python
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer, util

model = SentenceTransformer("sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2")

chunk_vecs = model.encode(chunks, normalize_embeddings=True)

query = "How do I reset my password?"
q_vec = model.encode(query, normalize_embeddings=True)

scores = util.dot_score(q_vec, chunk_vecs)[0]   # cosine, because normalized
top = scores.topk(3)
context = "\n".join(chunks[i] for i in top.indices)
```

Notice `normalize_embeddings=True`: once every vector has length 1, the plain **dot product equals cosine similarity** â€” a cheaper operation, and the reason vector databases love normalized embeddings. The 384 dimensions MiniLM produces are small enough that scoring thousands of chunks takes milliseconds on a laptop CPU, which is exactly why local pipelines like Homie ship it as the default embedder.

### Step 3: Don't Retrieve Garbage

Top-k always returns *something* â€” even when nothing matches. A query about cooking will still get its 3 "best" chunks from your networking docs, and the LLM will dutifully hallucinate a connection. Production retrievers add a **score threshold**: if the best chunk scores below roughly 0.3â€“0.4 cosine, say "no relevant context found" instead of feeding noise downstream. An honest empty answer beats a confident wrong one.

### Why This Model, Here?

Retrieval runs on every single query, often over thousands of chunks â€” latency and cost live here, not in the LLM call. all-MiniLM-L6-v2 is 80MB, runs offline via PyTorch or ONNX, and sits at the sweet spot of the speed/quality curve: strong enough that upgrading the embedder is rarely the first fix, small enough to embed your whole knowledge base in seconds.

> **Key Insight:** RAG quality is decided before the LLM sees a single token. Chunk with overlap so answers can't hide in the gaps, normalize so dot product becomes cosine, retrieve top-k, and refuse to answer when the best score is still bad. The retriever is four small functions â€” and it's where most RAG bugs actually live.

instruction.en: Now build the chunker that feeds the retriever. Write `chunk_words(words, size, overlap)` that slides a window of `size` words along the list, stepping forward `size - overlap` words each time, and returns each window joined into a string with spaces. Stop after the first window that reaches the end of the list. Print `chunk_words(["RAG", "splits", "documents", "into", "overlapping", "chunks", "first"], 4, 2)` â€” note how "documents into" and "overlapping chunks" each appear in two chunks: that's the overlap doing its job.

assert chunk_words(["RAG", "splits", "documents", "into", "overlapping", "chunks", "first"], 4, 2) == ['RAG splits documents into', 'documents into overlapping chunks', 'overlapping chunks first'], f"wrong windows: {chunk_words(['RAG', 'splits', 'documents', 'into', 'overlapping', 'chunks', 'first'], 4, 2)}"
assert chunk_words(["a", "b", "c"], 5, 2) == ['a b c'], "if size covers the whole list, return one chunk"
assert chunk_words(["a", "b", "c", "d"], 2, 0) == ['a b', 'c d'], "overlap=0 means back-to-back windows"
assert chunk_words(["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"], 2, 1) == ['a b', 'b c', 'c d', 'd e'], "overlap=1 repeats one word per boundary"
